en: The Discourse on Marvelous Qualities [0] Thus have I heard: at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Bamboo Grove, at the Kalandaka Feeding Ground.
[1] Then the venerable Ānanda, having dressed in the forenoon and taken his bowl and robe, entered Rājagṛha for alms.

As the venerable Ānanda was walking for alms through the city of Rājagṛha from house to house, he saw in a certain place a gabled hall with eighty doors, plastered and whitewashed, with banners and flags raised aloft and clusters of silk ribbons and garlands suspended from it.
Upon seeing it, this thought occurred to him: "Whatever faithful son or daughter of good family..."

Having caused such a gabled hall to be built, one might offer it to the Saṅgha of monks in the four directions; or, one might establish for the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One, a stūpa the size of an *āmalaka* fruit, erect a pillar the size of a needle,
set up a parasol the size of a jujube leaf, or fashion an image the size of a barley grain or a mustard seed.
"Whoever were to establish a relic, which of these two would produce the greater merit?
Then, this thought occurred to the Venerable Ānanda: "The Teacher is present before me; the Sugata is present before me.
Suppose I were to report this very matter to the Blessed One, so that I may remember it exactly as the Blessed One explains it to me."

[2] Then the Venerable Ānanda, having walked for alms through the city of Rājagṛha in the prescribed manner, having finished his meal and returned from his alms-round after the meal, set aside his bowl and robe, washed his feet, and approached the Blessed One.
Having approached, he bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and stood to one side. Standing to one side, the Venerable Ānanda [addressed] the Blessed One.

He said this: "Venerable sir, having dressed in the forenoon and taken my bowl and robes, I entered Rājagṛha for alms. While walking for alms through the city of Rājagṛha in regular succession, I saw in a certain place a gabled hall with eighty doors, plastered and whitewashed, with flags and banners raised high, and hung with bundles of silk ribbons and garlands."

And having seen this, it occurred to me once again: "If any faithful son of good family or daughter of good family were to offer such a gabled pavilion to the Saṅgha of monks in the four directions, or if one were to erect for the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha who has entered parinirvāṇa a stūpa made from a lump of clay the size of an *āmalaka* fruit, with a staff the thickness of a needle— "

"One might raise a parasol the size of a jujube leaf, or have an image made the size of a barley grain, or establish a relic the size of a mustard seed. Of these two, which would produce the greater merit?

Then this thought occurred to me: "The Teacher is present before me; the Sugata is present before me. Suppose I were to report this very matter to the Blessed One, so that the Blessed One himself may explain it."
"I shall uphold it thus.
When this was said, the Blessed One spoke to the venerable Ānanda: "Excellent, excellent, Ānanda! You have set out, Ānanda, for the benefit of many people and for the happiness of many people."

Out of compassion for the world, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of gods and humans, it is well that you consider this very matter to be worthy of inquiry of the Tathāgata. Therefore, Ānanda, listen and attend closely and well;
I shall speak. For Jambūdvīpa, Ānanda, is seven thousand yojanas in length and breadth, and it is broad toward the north.
To the south, facing like the front of a cart, some faithful son of good family or daughter of good family might fashion it out of the seven precious gems and offer it to the stream-enterers,

once-returners, non-returners, arhats, and pratyekabuddhas, or to the community of monks from the four directions; or [one might offer it] to the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly awakened one, who has passed into parinirvāṇa.

If one were to erect a stūpa the size of an *āmalaka* fruit from a lump of clay, or raise a staff the size of a needle, or set up a parasol the size of a jujube leaf, or have an image made the size of a barley grain, or enshrine a relic the size of a mustard seed— Ānanda, I declare that this latter [act] produces far more merit than that.

[4] Let alone, Ānanda, the continent of Jambūdvīpa. There is, Ānanda, a continent named Pūrvavideha, eight thousand yojanas in length and breadth, shaped like a half-moon on all sides. Suppose some faithful son of good family or daughter of good family were to make it out of the seven precious gems and offer it to the Saṅgha of monks from the four directions, or to a Tathāgata, an Arhat.
After a Perfectly Awakened One has passed into parinirvāṇa, if one were to erect a stūpa from a lump of clay the size of an *āmalaka* fruit,
set up a staff as thin as a needle, place a parasol the size of a jujube leaf, fashion an image the size of a barley grain,
and enshrine a relic the size of a mustard seed— Ānanda, I declare that this latter merit is far greater than the former.

[5] Let alone, Ānanda, the continent of Jambūdvīpa. There is, Ānanda, a continent named Aparagodānīya, nine thousand yojanas in length and breadth, shaped like the full moon on all sides. Suppose some faithful son of good family or daughter of good family were to make this [continent] out of the seven precious gems and offer it to the Saṅgha of monks from the four directions. Whoever...

Or, if one were to erect for a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksambuddha who has entered parinirvāṇa a stūpa made from a lump of clay the size of an āmalaka fruit, set up a staff the thickness of a needle, place a parasol the size of a jujube leaf, have an image made the size of a barley grain, or enshrine a relic the size of a mustard seed— Ānanda, I declare that this latter merit is far more abundant than the former.
[6] Let alone, Ānanda, the continent of Jambūdvīpa; let alone the continent of Pūrvavideha; let alone the continent of Avaragodānīya.

There is, Ānanda, a continent named Uttarakuru, ten thousand yojanas in length and breadth, square on all sides. Suppose some son of good family or daughter of good family, endowed with faith, were to make it out of the seven precious gems...

Or, having prepared [an offering] as large as the fourfold community of monks, one might dedicate it; or one might establish for the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One who has entered parinirvāṇa, a stūpa made from a lump of clay the size of an *āmalaka* fruit,
erect a staff the thickness of a needle, place a parasol the size of a jujube leaf, or fashion an image the size of a barley grain or even the size of a mustard seed.
I declare that one who would establish a relic would produce far more merit than that.
[7] Let alone, Ānanda, the continent of Jambūdvīpa; let alone the continent of Pūrvavideha; let alone the continent of Avaragodānīya;
let alone the continent of Uttarakuru. There exists, Ānanda, the Vaijayanta palace of Śakra, the lord of the gods.

There is a palace named [such-and-such]. Suppose some faithful son of good family or daughter of good family were to construct it out of the seven precious gems and offer it to the community of monks from the four directions; or suppose someone else, after the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One has passed into parinirvāṇa, were to establish a stūpa made from a lump of clay the size of an *āmalaka* fruit, with a staff the thickness of a needle.

One might raise a parasol the size of a jujube leaf, have an image made the size of a barley grain, and enshrine a relic the size of a mustard seed—Ānanda, I declare that this latter merit is far more abundant than the former. [8] Let alone Ānanda, the continent of Jambūdvīpa; let alone the continent of Pūrvavideha; let alone Avaragodānīya.

It is an island. Let alone the continent of Uttarakuru; let alone Vaijayanta, the palace of Śakra, the lord of the gods. Ānanda, there exists this triple-thousand great-thousandfold world system. Suppose some faithful son of good family or daughter of good family were to make it out of the seven precious jewels and offer it to stream-enterers, once-returners, and non-returners...

Whether one were to dedicate [merit] to the Arhats, the Pratyekabuddhas, or even to the Saṅgha of monks from the four quarters; or whether one were to erect for the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha who has entered Parinirvāṇa, a stūpa made from a lump of clay the size of an *āmalaka* fruit,
set up a staff the thickness of a needle, a parasol the size of a jujube leaf, or a statue the size of a barley grain— [the latter would be superior].
One should have made [an image] the size of a mustard seed and establish it as a relic; Ānanda, I declare that this very merit is far more abundant than that.

Why is that? For, Ānanda, the Tathāgata is immeasurable through generosity, immeasurable through ethical discipline, immeasurable through patience, immeasurable through vigor, immeasurable through renunciation, immeasurable through loving-kindness, immeasurable through compassion, immeasurable through sympathetic joy, and immeasurable through equanimity.

“Ānanda, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is indeed endowed with immeasurable and incalculable qualities by virtue of the four grounds of self-confidence, the ten powers of a Tathāgata, and the eighteen unique attributes of a Buddha.
When this had been said, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the Blessed One as follows:

“It is marvelous, Blessed One! It is marvelous, Sugata, how wonderful this Dharma-discourse is! What is the name of this Dharma-discourse? And how should I remember it? “Therefore, Ānanda, you should remember this Dharma-discourse as ‘The Marvelous,’ a Dharma-discourse of marvels. Thus spoke the Blessed One. The monks and the Venerable Ānanda were uplifted and rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said.
They rejoiced in what was spoken.
